newsitem.title: BOSNIA: No extradition of war criminals - Bosnian Serbs.
newsitem.headline: No extradition of war criminals - Bosnian Serbs.

text.p: The president of the Bosnian Serb Republic, Biljana Plavsic, reiterated on Tuesday her commitment to the Dayton peace agreement but baulked at extraditing indicted war criminals, a cornerstone of the accord.
She said the Bosnian Serb constitution forbade the extradition of Serb citizens, the Bosnian Serb news agency SRNA reported.
Plavsic was speaking at a news conference on her meetings with NATO alliance leaders in the Portuguese town of Sintra last week.
Plavsic met U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright in Banja Luka, the main Bosnian Serb city, on Sunday.

Albright made a whirlwind tour of Croatia, Yugoslavia and Bosnia last weekend demanding from Moslem, Serb and Croat leaders that they stick to the letter of the Dayton accord which ended the war in Bosnia in 1995.
Extradition of war criminals to an international war crimes court in The Hague is one of the highlights of a new U.S. policy to reinvigorate the faltering peace treaty.
Plavsic argued that the extradition of citizens of the Bosnian Serb Republic was banned under its constitution.

"Albright replied that the Dayton Agreement was above the Serb Republic constitution, to which I said that our constitution had been harmonized with the peace agreement at a session of the Serb Republic People's Assembly," she said, quoted by SRNA.
The war crimes tribunal in The Hague has indicted 75 people -- the majority of them Serbs followed by Croats and Moslems -- but only nine are in custody.
The two most notorious indictees, former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic and his army commander General Ratko Mladic, are still at large.
Bosnian Serb sources there was no Serb politician who would dare extradite the two men.
"There is not a single politician who would dare do that. He and his family would be ostracised for 10 generations to come," former Banja Luka mayor Predrag Radic told Reuters.
The 30,000-strong, NATO-led peace force in Bosnia says it has no mandate to hunt down and capture indicted war criminals.

Plavsic said the most important characteristic of the Sintra meeting was the fact that, "in addition to warnings sent to the Serbs and Croats, the Moslems were warned for the first time that their aspirations to dominate and outvote (post-war Bosnia) would not be tolerated", the agency said.

Bosnia was reconstituted as a single state under the Dayton accords but is effectively partitioned into autonomous Serb and Moslem-Croat entities which resist cooperation and central institutions set up in Sarajevo.
